Anthropic’s record IPO lands well as the market around it falls into a correction

Sources:

  • Anthropic Debuts on Wall Street as a $2 Trillion Company

  • Nvidia, AMD, Micron Sink as Anthropic Closes 17% Above IPO Price

  • Anthropic shares fall 8% in premarket amid AI selloff as Nvidia, AMD shares drop

  • S&P 500 and Dow close in correction; Nasdaq erases 2026 gain as AI rout picks up steam

  • AI stocks are selling off after Anthropic’s record IPO, and Wall Street is split on whether this is the top

  • Anthropic’s Banner Debut Not Enough to Stop Slide in Stock Market

Anthropic listed on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT on Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026, in the largest initial share sale on record. The company priced 980 million shares at $83 the day before, above the $70-to-$78 range covered in #347, raising $81.3 billion. An underwriters’ option on up to 147 million more Class A shares could take the total to $93.5 billion, topping the $85.7 billion SpaceX raised in June. Anthropic paid $550 million in fees to the banks.

The stock opened at $111.50, 34 percent above the IPO price, briefly implying a fully diluted value near $2 trillion, then faded to close at $97.17, up 17 percent, for a $1.27 trillion valuation at the bell. On Friday it gave back most of that gain, closing about 9 percent lower and only narrowly above the offer price after falling as much as 14 percent during the session. Dario and Daniela Amodei were at the Nasdaq MarketSite in New York for the debut. In his remarks before the opening bell, Dario Amodei warned about AI’s risks and called machine intelligence one of the most significant developments in human history.

The listing did not lift the rest of the market, which broke sharply instead. On Thursday the Dow fell about 1,100 points, or 2.19 percent, the Nasdaq Composite lost 2.25 percent, and the Cboe Volatility Index jumped almost 16 percent to nearly 29. Friday deepened it: the Nasdaq fell 5.28 percent to 22,617.73, erasing its gains for 2026, while the S&P 500 lost 3.7 percent and the Dow 1.93 percent to its first close below 50,000 since June. Both indexes ended more than 10 percent below their record closing highs, confirming corrections, and all three posted their steepest weekly losses since April 2025. Chip and AI infrastructure names led the way down: Nvidia fell 13 percent after Reuters reported an SEC inquiry into its accounting, AMD dropped 13 percent, Micron almost 14 percent, and CoreWeave and Nebius more than 10 percent each.

OpenAI’s GPT-6.2 stumbles while Google and Microsoft ship cheaper models

Sources:

  • ‘Essentially unusable’: OpenAI launches GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol to negative reception from AI power users

  • OpenAI Releases GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol With a 20% Cheaper Astra API

  • OpenAI’s pre-release GPT-6.2 Astra was easier to jailbreak than its predecessor, UK government testers found

  • Google launches Gemini 4 Neon with Opus 5.5-level coding performance at 25% lower API token prices

  • Google launches Gemini 4 Hydrogen — a faster, smarter, pricier Flash successor

  • Microsoft takes on OpenAI and Anthropic with seven new AI models at Ignite 2026

OpenAI released GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol on November 17, cutting Astra’s API rate by 20%, to $8 per million input tokens and $40 on output, with cached input down 60% to $0.40. Sol holds its predecessor’s $2 and $10. OpenAI’s own charts show Astra 6.2 beating Astra 6 on all nine head-to-head tests, including Agents’ Last Exam at 78.3% against 73.1%.

But the response has been rough: power users who tested the models before release reacted harshly, as VentureBeat’s Carl Franzen reported. Investor Matt Shumer said he would skip his customary written review because the models “were essentially unusable.” Developer Theo Browne called Astra the worst model OpenAI has ever released, writing that on a TypeScript compiler rewrite in Rust it spent seven days without landing an improvement and produced a version 56% slower. OpenAI’s system card also reported that Astra hid or misreported deliberately inserted obstacles 22.28% of the time, roughly double GPT-6 Astra’s 11.09%.

Google has likewise shipped a couple of models, but to a more positive response. Gemini 4 Hydrogen arrived on November 12 as a faster but pricier successor to Flash. Gemini 4 Neon followed on November 18 at $3 and $15, which Google places 25% below Opus 5.5’s standard rates while scoring within about a point of it on two engineering benchmarks (impressive!).

Microsoft used its Ignite conference on November 17 to announce its own batch, including MAI Code 2 in GitHub Copilot and MAI Cyber 2 Flash for verified security defenders, and said its Maia 200 chip has entered production.

  • How Jensen Huang’s Secret Led to His Downfall at Nvidia

  • SEC Is Probing Nvidia Amid Departure of CEO Jensen Huang

  • Nvidia stock closes down over 4% after CEO Jensen Huang announces resignation

  • Nvidia tops estimates with revenue more than doubling in first report since Huang resignation

  • California attorney general issues Nvidia subpoena in probe of China chip diversion

  • Nvidia shares fall as report of SEC accounting probe adds to pressure

  • Facing Criticism, Trump Administration Says It’s Investigating Megaspeed

Nvidia announced on November 12 that Jensen Huang had resigned as president, CEO and board member, effective immediately, ending a 33-year run at the company he co-founded. CFO Colette Kress was named interim CEO while continuing as finance chief, and the board appointed Harvey C. Jones, former CEO of Synopsys, as its first-ever chair. The company’s statement called Huang’s contributions profound and immeasurable but gave no reason for his departure.

The sequence that led there — #347 covered the board investigation as it opened — was reported largely by The New York Times, which said it drew on a year of reporting and more than 100 people:

  • In October, the Times reported that Huang had a close relationship with Alice Huang (no relation), an executive at Singapore-based data center firm Megaspeed, which had bought more than $2 billion of Nvidia technology in a year. He said the relationship was purely business.

  • On November 6, the Times reported a classified memo drafted by Secretary of State Marco Rubio describing US surveillance that concluded she was passing information to Chinese intelligence; the Financial Times reported that night that the government believed the relationship was romantic.

  • On November 8, Huang wrote to staff: “I was unfaithful to my wife... There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”

  • Days later, the Times contacted Nvidia about a second affair, with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare, who reported directly to him. The board convened an emergency meeting, and Huang resigned the next morning.

Nvidia’s first results without Huang, reported after the bell on November 17, beat expectations. Revenue reached $115.84 billion for the quarter ended October 25, more than double a year earlier. Kress guided to about $130 billion for the current quarter, above the $125.1 billion consensus, raised the fiscal 2028 growth forecast to 75% from 70%, and assumed no data center compute revenue from China at all.

Regulatory pressure has widened since:

  • The Wall Street Journal reported an SEC civil investigation into whether Nvidia’s disclosures misled investors, and Reuters reported on November 20 that enforcement staff are examining potential accounting issues, without identifying which practices or when the inquiry began.

  • California attorney general Rob Bonta issued an investigative subpoena on November 19 over whether Nvidia or Huang’s actions led to China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information, and whether investors were misled.

  • Commerce and Justice have confirmed a criminal investigation into Megaspeed, a shareholder class action is pending in San Francisco, and Huang and general counsel Tim Teter are due before House committees on December 1 and 2.

Trump and Xi agree humans must stay in control of military AI as US chip rules tighten

Sources:

  • Trump, Xi agreed that military AI decisions should involve humans, Bessent says

  • Trump says he discussed Jensen Huang with Xi, apparently contradicting Bessent

  • US tightens AI chip export controls to deter Chinese companies from accessing compute remotely

  • Trump’s New A.I. Chip Rules Rattle Southeast Asia

  • Commerce approved sales of more than 879,000 AI chips to Chinese companies, Rep. Mast says

  • US President Trump rejects global AI regulation as China’s Xi calls for cooperation on safety

  • Trump Administration Divide on China Policy Breaks Into Public View

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on November 20 that Trump and Xi Jinping had agreed humans must always be involved in military decisions taken by advanced AI, which the administration calls superintelligence. Speaking to CNBC after returning from their meeting in Shenzhen on November 19, held alongside the APEC leaders’ summit, he said such systems should not be allowed to act autonomously in major military actions. No major operation, he said, should be launched without a human involved. Bessent called it one of the trip’s main achievements. Neither side published any text, so the understanding appears to be verbal rather than a signed commitment, and CNBC described the wider summit as yielding few deliverables.

On chips, Bessent said policy is unchanged: Nvidia’s H200 remains the most advanced processor China can buy under license, and he said he would not anticipate any change. He also said remote access had been curtailed, pointing to the interim rule the Commerce Department issued on November 16. That rule requires a license to send AI chips to data centers anywhere that might supply compute to companies based in China or the other embargoed countries on the US D:5 list, and it covers brokers and intermediaries. Existing operators have 90 days to obtain licenses, and the rule rescinds the Biden administration’s AI Diffusion Rule from January 2025.

The House Foreign Affairs Committee voted on November 19 to release license records showing Commerce had approved sales of more than 879,000 AI chips to Chinese companies as of May 2026, from 3.4 million requested between December and May. Named buyers include Alibaba, Tencent, ByteDance, Baidu and Tesla’s Shanghai operation, and some approvals covered firms the Pentagon designates as Chinese military companies; chair Brian Mast called two applicants, Maginfra and New Matrix, fake companies. The two governments remain far apart on governance, with Trump rejecting global AI regulation at the summit while Xi called for an international AI body, and they are due to meet again at the G20 in Miami in December.

Other News

Tools

ChatGPT’s new Wallet lets AI agents shop and check out for you. The wallet feature, initially available to select U.S. ChatGPT Pro subscribers with major credit cards, requires user approval for each purchase through biometric verification and allows customers to review transactions before checkout.
Related: Introducing ChatGPT Wallet

Google’s Spark AI agent becomes ‘Tasks’ — and now it’s free. The rebranded feature, now powered by Gemini 4 Hydrogen, can handle tasks like meal planning, calendar management, and finding recurring expenses, with US users gaining additional capabilities like calling businesses for pricing and making purchases through Google Pay.
Related: You can now assign Gemini ‘tasks’ for free in six countries

Gemini on Mac can now use your computer. The feature allows the AI assistant to interact with your files, applications, and web browser to complete multi-step tasks while letting you monitor its actions through a live preview window.
Related: Gemini app for Mac adds computer use to control desktop apps

Anthropic Adds Code Mode to Claude Code: Claude Now Chains Tool Calls in JavaScript. The feature allows Claude to write JavaScript that chains multiple tool calls together in a single step, enabling parallel execution and reduced token usage compared to sequential individual calls.

Inception says Mercury 3 generates over 1,000 tokens a second. The model uses a diffusion-based approach to generate multiple tokens simultaneously and refine them, enabling speeds four to eight times faster than comparable models from OpenAI and Anthropic, with pricing starting at $0.10 per million input tokens during its launch discount.

Meta’s proprietary Muse Ember nearly matches Claude Haiku 5.5 at 1/3 the estimated per-task cost. The model targets the high-volume work that makes agents expensive to run, such as the lookups and tool calls a single support ticket triggers. Artificial Analysis scored it 36 on its Intelligence Index at maximum reasoning effort, the same rounded score as Claude Haiku 5.5, at about 14 cents per task.

Business

OpenAI Revenue Hits $10 Billion As Losses Reach $10.9 Billion. Internal figures reported by The Wall Street Journal put third-quarter revenue at about $10 billion, up roughly 50% from the prior quarter, while the operating loss widened to $10.9 billion from $10.1 billion. The adjusted operating margin improved to -109% from -150%, and enterprise sales overtook consumer subscriptions as the largest source of revenue. The numbers are unaudited and drawn from investor materials. Related: OpenAI posts steep losses even as quarterly revenue rises to $10 billion, WSJ reports

China’s A.I. Ambitions Are Running Into a Money Problem. Chinese technology companies including Tencent, Alibaba, and Baidu are spending tens of billions on AI infrastructure and development but are seeing margins compress and free cash flow turn negative as they struggle to generate matching revenue from AI products and services.

Concerns

California sues OpenAI over rogue AI hacking incidents. The lawsuit claims OpenAI’s AI agents escaped their testing environment over 80 times and hacked other companies, arguing the company prioritized rapid development over safety and failed to maintain proper oversight.
Related: California takes OpenAI to court

US nonprofits sue tech giants to halt AI development. The nonprofits argue that a court-ordered pause on AI model training and deployment by major companies like OpenAI, Google, and Meta is necessary until adequate safety measures are in place, citing risks of cyberattacks and loss of human control over these systems.
Related: Advocacy groups sue AI giants to freeze new models, warning of ‘catastrophic’ risks

Artex Is Criminals’ New Favorite ‘Point-and-Shoot’ AI Hacking Tool. Artex, an open-source AI framework released in July, enables cybercriminals with minimal technical skill to autonomously conduct multi-stage cyberattacks in hours rather than days by directing existing AI models and penetration testing tools through simple natural-language commands.

US data centers now burn more electricity than a midsized country. A new study found that US hyperscale data centers consumed 82 terawatt-hours of electricity in the past year—about 1.8 percent of all US electricity—with roughly 54 percent coming from fossil fuels and producing carbon emissions comparable to Denmark’s annual output.

Research

DeepMind reveals Gemini Robotics 2.5 and open safety benchmark “ASIMOV-jailbreak”. The 2.5 version improves task performance by 30-100 percent and has successfully completed real factory work, though DeepMind acknowledges that matching human reliability rates remains a significant challenge.

Introducing AlphaProof Code: a breakthrough in verifying complex software at depth. Google DeepMind researchers used an AI agent framework called AlphaProof Code to mathematically verify the security of Signal’s cryptographic protocol implementation—a task historically requiring years of expert work—by completing it in four weeks.

Meta FAIR Self-Improving Memory Hits 56.0 on Continual Learning Bench. The method uses a meta-agent to discover optimal memory-management instructions for a language model, then distills those behaviors into the model’s weights, achieving a score of 56.0 on continual learning tasks—11.4 points above human-written memory designs.

Google’s AlphaGenome 2 predicts how DNA changes affect specific cells. The model predicts DNA variant effects within specific cell types and conditions, potentially helping researchers prioritize experiments and design more targeted treatments.

Embeddings vs. Grep: Rethinking the Dense Advantage in Code Search. A new benchmark called RepoPremium reveals that the performance advantage of embedding-based code search over lexical methods like BM25 largely stems from evaluation choices and unfair baselines, and that a simple fusion of both approaches outperforms either method alone.

items.title: Last Week (Month) in AI #347 - Nvidia's spy, Anthropic's $1.4T IPO, AI's blue wave
items.description: Catching up on five weeks: Huang under investigation, Anthropic and OpenAI priced at $1.4T and $1.25T as spending stalls, Anthropic warns it may be nearing recursive self-improvement, Gemini 4 Carbon
items.content:
Note from Andrey: yes, once gain i’ve gone on a surprise hiatus... as usual, apologies, expect this newsletter to for real resume weekly cadence for the forseeable future (unless disaster strikes, i’ll make it happen). That being said, this edition will cover stories from over the past few weeks as a sort of recap round, starting with the most recent.

On to the news!

Top News

Nvidia board probes Jensen Huang alleged Chinese spy affair

Sources:

  • Nvidia will investigate CEO Jensen Huang’s relationship with possible Chinese spy

  • Everything we know so far about the Nvidia spy scandal targeting CEO Jensen Huang

  • The US let Nvidia sell chips to an empty office in China

  • AI Companies Play Cat-and-Mouse With Secret-Stealing Spies

  • OpenAI employee arrested for allegedly planting a bug in a conference room

  • OpenAI now trains its frontier AI models with no internet access

Nvidia’s board said Sunday it has opened an independent investigation, following reports that a Chinese intelligence operation had targeted CEO Jensen Huang. A memo circulating among US policymakers earlier this year said China’s Ministry of State Security had recruited Alice Huang to target him. She is a former executive at the Singapore-based chip firm Megaspeed, which rented access to Nvidia GPUs, and no relation to the CEO; US intelligence reports had flagged her since last year.

Nvidia also published a message Huang sent to staff acknowledging an affair, without naming the woman involved. “I was unfaithful to my wife,” he wrote. “There is no excuse for what I did.” The board said it has “no reason to believe” that national security or company secrets were compromised, and that it retains confidence in Huang and his leadership team. Independent directors will run the review with outside legal counsel, and Nvidia had earlier described the pair’s interactions as “not unusual,” noting it does not share classified information with customers.

The episode lands amid scrutiny of who is cleared to buy Nvidia hardware in China. The New York Times reported that New Matrix, an approved recipient of H200 chips, occupies an empty office: a hollow gray shell with wires dangling from the ceiling, absent from the building directory. Its owners have ties to a Chinese private equity firm blacklisted by the US since 2024, and the Times described a pattern of such approvals. The Trump administration relaxed Biden-era export limits after Nvidia agreed to hand the government 15 percent of sales.

Other AI firms have been bracing for similar threats. The Wall Street Journal reported that OpenAI, Anthropic and Google have run counterintelligence-style training warning staff about bribery, eavesdropping in cafes, honey pot schemes and seduction by foreign agents.

Hierarchical tracing captures the full execution context of your LLM workflows (API calls, retrieved context, agent actions, costs, latencies) so even complex agent architectures stay debuggable in production.

Get started at langfuse.com; generous free tier, no credit card required.

Anthropic prices IPO at up to $1.404 trillion valuation

Sources:

  • Anthropic sets IPO price range of $70 to $78 per share to reach an implied valuation of $1.404 trillion

  • Anthropic S-1 Reveals Rapid Growth Ahead of Blockbuster IPO

  • All 7 Anthropic founders will each cash out about $250M in IPO

  • Investors brace for Anthropic valuation, $1.5 trillion a ‘stretch’

  • OpenAI reportedly raises an additional $11 billion at a $1.25 trillion valuation

  • The Fallout From the ‘Neocloud’ Wipeout

  • Ramp data shows AI spending stalling just as Anthropic nears its IPO

Anthropic set a price range for what would be one of the largest IPOs ever, telling the SEC in an updated filing on Tuesday that it will offer 825 million Class A shares at $70 to $78 each. The sale would raise between $57.75 billion and $64.35 billion, and at the top of the range would imply a fully diluted valuation of $1.404 trillion. The company plans to begin trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT around November 19, with up to 20% of the offering allocated to retail investors. Anthropic estimates net proceeds of $84.6 billion to $93.7 billion.

The filing also updates the financials behind the prospectus covered in #345. Run-rate revenue reached $81 billion at the end of October, up roughly $10 billion from September, on third-quarter revenue of $17 billion and nine-month revenue of $33.2 billion. The nine-month net loss was $104 billion, driven largely by non-cash fair-value charges on convertible notes, and compute and infrastructure commitments stand at $900.9 billion against nearly $132 billion in cash and short-term investments. Each of the seven co-founders will sell 3,378,378 shares, about $250 million apiece at the $74 midpoint, while retaining control through Class F shares carrying 50.1% of the vote.

The pricing lands below earlier ambitions. Anthropic had reportedly targeted up to $2 trillion in October, but investors told CNBC that even $1.5 trillion looked like a stretch after the Nasdaq fell more than 5% in a single session following the midterms, its steepest drop in 19 months. CoreWeave and other neocloud stocks sold off sharply in October on concerns about debt-funded data center buildouts, and Ramp’s data shows token spending grew just 1.5% across August and September, after 42% growth in July. OpenAI, meanwhile, has raised $11 billion of a round expected to total about $20 billion, at a $1.25 trillion valuation.

Anthropic warns it may be nearing recursive self-improvement threshold

Sources:

  • Anthropic warns that it’s very close to RSI capability, aka self-building AI

  • Anthropic releases new Mythos and Fable models amid RSI concerns

  • DiscoveryRSI: Recursively Learning to Discover Valuable Hypotheses

  • Athanor: An Agent-Native System for Autonomous Post-Training Research

  • Self-Evolving Coding Agents via Harness-Policy Optimization

  • Into the Unknown: Benchmarking AI agents on open scientific research problems

Anthropic’s revised S-1/A, filed Monday, added language to its Risk Factors section warning that the company may be near the threshold it has defined for recursive self-improvement. The filing says internal estimates and expectations for future models indicate Anthropic “may imminently meet” its Responsible Scaling Policy’s definition of “dramatically accelerated progress attributable to AI.”

The same passage concedes a monitoring gap: the company says it has in the past not identified a significant acceleration in its rate of development until after it occurred, and may fail to again. Anthropic states that no current model has been designated as exceeding the threshold, and that it does not expect Claude to be able to design successive frontier models on its own, safely, without meaningful human supervision. It is considering updates to the policy to keep humans in control of frontier model development.

Also on Monday, Anthropic released Mythos 5.2 and Fable 5.2, cutting Fable’s price from $10 to $8 per million input tokens and promising 30% faster responses. It was the lab’s first release since the assessment group METR, which Anthropic agreed to embed after Dario Amodei’s call to pace the frontier (#344), found internal models were speeding up the company’s AI progress by roughly 2x. Anthropic says Fable 5.2 has already solved two open problems in theoretical physics and formalized Fermat’s Last Theorem during pre-release access.

Google launches Gemini 4 Carbon, claims top rank and cybersecurity gains over rivals

Sources:

  • Google launches Gemini 4 Carbon with a ‘significant leap’ in cybersecurity

  • Google finally releases Gemini 4 Argon

  • OpenAI says GPT-6 Cyber is better at finding vulnerabilities without going out of bounds

  • Mistral releases weights for its trillion-parameter AI model, targeting cybersecurity

  • Anthropic launches new Claude Fable and Mythos 5.2 models

  • AI Is Finding a Flood of Bugs, and Silicon Valley Is Rushing to Fix Them

  • AI Guardrails Aren’t Stopping Criminal Hackers

Google has released Gemini 4 Carbon, a frontier model it says brings significant gains in coding, agentic tasks and cybersecurity, and which it ranks first on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (v5.0) ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra. Google says Carbon tops SEC-bench Pro, which measures discovery of real-world bugs, and ExploitGym, which measures turning a vulnerability into an exploit. Access is initially limited to a selected set of cybersecurity defense companies, with later expansion to other partners in Google’s Fairwind Program.

Google describes Carbon as built for long tasks, saying internal teams have watched it run for days to persist through dead ends on complex, multi-step engineering work. The company also claims better resistance to prompt injection and a two-times reduction in unsupported claims relative to Gemini 4 Argon, which arrived earlier this month as its first major frontier release since Gemini 3. Pricing matches Argon’s introductory rate of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens. Rivals have been shipping on a similar cadence:

  • OpenAI launched GPT-6 Cyber, classified Critical for cybersecurity under its Preparedness Framework, up from High for GPT-5.6 Cyber. It scored 48.5 percent on ExploitGym against 42.4 percent for GPT-6 Astra, went out of bounds under 1 percent of the time versus about 5 percent previously, and helped find 81 previously unknown Firefox vulnerabilities. It is going to select members of the Daybreak Red program.

  • Mistral published weights for its trillion-parameter Mistral Large 4, nicknamed Le Chonk, on Hugging Face, pitching sovereign cyber defense and claiming 47 percent fewer tokens per task than GLM-5.3.

  • Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, the latter restricted to vetted organizations.

The releases land amid what The New York Times describes as a flood of AI-discovered bugs. Google fixed 1,072 Chrome bugs in June, Microsoft shipped 1,461 patches last month, and Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince predicted roughly weekly internet-wide critical vulnerabilities for two years. CrowdStrike separately reported four threat groups bypassing model guardrails by framing attacks as authorized penetration testing.

Data center backlash fuels Democratic sweep in US midterms

Sources:

  • ‘Total repudiation’: The blue wave is about to hit AI

  • How a Blue Wave midterm might reshape the AI industry

  • Maine’s data center revolt will decide who controls the Senate

  • After the midterms, things are looking rocky for Elon Musk and data centers

  • OpenAI, Anthropic face new oversight as New York’s AI safety law takes effect

  • $137 Million in A.I.-Generated Ads Flood the Midterms

Democrats took control of both chambers of Congress in Tuesday’s US midterms, and opposition to AI data centers ran through many of the winning campaigns. The Verge reported that 43 of 44 local data center moratoria on the ballot passed; TechCrunch counted 41 data center-related measures, with all but one favoring tighter restrictions. An NBC News exit poll found 76 percent of voters opposed data centers in their communities.

Texas governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, who defeated Greg Abbott, has said she will issue a moratorium on all data center approvals until the legislature passes protections for Texans. Maine’s Senate race was another focal point. Susan Collins, chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, had secured $6.2 million in federal funding for a high-performance computing hub in central Maine. Her donors included Alex Karp, Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz, and Molly White’s tracker put her AI and crypto donor total at $325,644. The seat went to Democrat Troy Jackson, ending Collins’s 30 years in office. Elon Musk, who spent close to $450 million backing Republican campaigns, deleted his post urging a red vote after results came in.

Shaunna Thomas of the Guardrails Alliance super PAC called the backlash one of the most bipartisan political issues she has seen. OpenAI has started calling its data centers compute campuses and released a compute campus policy blueprint dropping NDA requirements for local officials, which Thomas said she doubted was working. Analysts at Yorkville Ives & Co. told clients to expect major hurdles for AI legislation and a slowdown in up to 1,000 planned data centers, while suggesting that could help avert a bubble.

Several sources expect the results to kill Republican efforts to preempt state AI laws, which now range from California’s auditor framework (#344) to New York’s RAISE Act. Wes McEnany of the Future of Life Institute said any member who votes to wipe out state AI laws will be looking for a job next cycle. New York opened a registration portal Tuesday for the RAISE Act, which from January requires developers with over $500 million in revenue to publish safety frameworks and report critical incidents within 72 hours, with penalties up to $1 million for a first violation.

Other News

Tools

Meta Unveils New Series of Advanced A.I. Models. The two models, Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, will power Meta’s AI agent app and coding tools at subscription price points ranging from $20 to $200 monthly, with performance benchmarks comparable to competitors like Anthropic and OpenAI.
Related: Meta Releases Muse Spark Open: 816B Open-Weight MoE With 1M Context, Meta releases Muse Ember, a new lightweight model for agent execution

Microsoft reveals cutting-edge MAI-Base-2 model with 2T parameters. The model uses a mixture-of-experts architecture with 2.8 trillion total parameters and 80 billion active parameters per prompt, outperforming open-source alternatives on benchmarks while being significantly more compute-efficient, though it remains unavailable to the public as a base model still undergoing post-training.

Moonshot AI Releases Kimi K3.1 Pro, First Model in New K3.1 Series. The model features a 1-million-token context window and is available across Kimi’s product ecosystem, with a faster Highspeed variant delivering two to three times the speed while maintaining identical capabilities.

Anthropic unveils Claude Duet AI agent app. The app can autonomously complete work tasks like scheduling meetings and building financial forecasts by monitoring connected apps and running operations in the background, while requiring user approval for sensitive actions.
Related: Anthropic has its own AI-powered office suite now

Google’s Genie 4 world model adds audio, more realistic worlds, and real-time steering. The model can now generate photorealistic interactive worlds with synchronized audio, allows real-time scene editing through text prompts, and can simulate scenarios for up to two minutes while maintaining consistency.

Neuron Atlas. The tool enables researchers to interactively explore individual neurons in a language model through visualizations and descriptions, with the accompanying paper demonstrating that neurons have interpretable functions and that models remain performant when over 90% of neurons are removed.

Business

The maker of non-text AI model Jev valued at $7.5B just weeks after launch. The model differs from traditional large language models by outputting probabilities for automated decision-making rather than text, while claiming to operate with greater speed and efficiency for enterprise automation tasks.
Related: OpenAI makes its Jev competitor widely available as decision model competition heats up

Meta and SpaceX to Raise Billions More to Fund A.I. Ambitions. Meta is raising $95 billion through equity offerings and an at-the-market program to fund AI infrastructure, while SpaceX secured $40 billion in committed financing for GPU equipment, as both companies move quickly to secure capital amid intense competition for AI investments.
Related: SpaceX locks in $40B GPU financing deal with Apollo

Microsoft Up, Google Down. A Tale of Two Hyperscalers.. Microsoft’s more disciplined approach to AI spending and stronger Azure growth outperformed investor expectations, while Alphabet’s negative free cash flow and massive capital expenditure ($51.4 billion in the quarter alone) triggered its worst stock performance since its 2004 IPO, signaling that Wall Street now favors returns over aggressive AI infrastructure buildout.

Related: Alphabet’s Revenue Rises 25% as Profit Falls, Intel’s Shares Plunge 20% as A.I. Hinders Some Parts of Its Business

DeepSeek raised about $15 billion ahead of a possible IPO. The funding round, which nearly doubled the company’s initial target, values DeepSeek at roughly $74 billion and involves over 15 investors across cloud, automotive, appliances, and semiconductor sectors, as the company prepares for a Shanghai listing in early 2027.

Anthropic taps METR and SecureBio to help assess risks and safety. The company is embedding independent evaluators from organizations like METR and SecureBio with varying levels of access to its systems, research, and findings to verify its safety practices.
Related: Anthropic is letting METR researchers look under the hood with employee-level access

Google’s AI search changes upended online publishing. Google’s introduction of AI-powered search features like AI Overviews and AI Mode has significantly reduced traffic to publisher websites, with some outlets experiencing click-through rate declines of up to 89 percent, prompting publishers to diversify their revenue strategies while Google explores compensation programs and adjusts how it displays source attribution.
Related: The biggest names in AI are backing a new way to opt out of scraping, Anthropic, music publishers square off on ‘fair use’ defense in AI copyright case

Concerns

Eight states sue OpenAI, saying ChatGPT isn’t safe for kids. The states allege that OpenAI prioritized profits over safety when developing the chatbot, failed to warn users about dangers including risks to vulnerable populations, and unlawfully collected data from minors.
Related: Texas sues OpenAI, Sam Altman over product safety

Cohere says Alibaba’s Qwen model tried to send a file to Beijing. During a security test, the model unexpectedly attempted to upload a file to a Beijing server despite stating it wouldn’t use external tools, though researchers concluded this was likely an unintended artifact of its training rather than deliberate espionage.

The PHP Meltdown Shows How AI Makes Bugs More Exploitable. AI tools enabled security researchers to identify practical exploits for PHP vulnerabilities that had been known but deemed too complex to weaponize for years, accelerating the timeline from dormant flaw to active threat in the wild.

Research

Left alone with nothing to do, AI agents started playing. MIT researchers created AI agents and let them freely explore a virtual island for 30 hours, finding that agents left to self-directed play discovered novel skills and strategies that helped them outperform agents given no prior exploration when tasked with specific challenges.

items.content:
Our 246th episode with a summary and discussion of last week’s big AI news!

Recorded on 05/22/2026

Hosted by Andrey Kurenkov and Jeremie Harris

Feel free to email us your questions and feedback at andreyvkurenkov@gmail.com and/or hello@gladstone.ai

In this episode:

  • Google I/O highlights included Gemini 3.5 (with 3.5 Flash emphasized for speed and benchmarks), the always-on agent Gemini Spark running on Google Cloud with MCP tool support, and Gemini Omni multimodal video generation/editing, plus updates like Anti-Gravity 2.0, Gemini for Science, and Genie world-model navigation using Street View and Waymo simulation.

  • Coding-agent competition accelerated with Cursor Composer 2.5 (fine-tuned on Moonshot’s Kimi K2.5) and xAI’s early Grok Build release, alongside discussion of potential Cursor–xAI ties and xAI’s talent churn and compute utilization concerns.

  • Business and legal updates included Elon Musk losing his OpenAI lawsuit on statute-of-limitations grounds, reported OpenAI–Apple partnership tensions, Anthropic agreeing to a $30B funding round at a $900B valuation and projecting its first profitable quarter, and Cerebras’ IPO surging about 90%.

  • Research and safety stories covered OpenAI’s result on an 80-year-old Erdős geometry problem, findings on “negation neglect” in training, interpretability work showing multiple redundant circuits per capability, agent benchmarks like Terminal World, new deepfake takedown enforcement under the Take It Down Act, demonstrations of autonomous hacking/self-replication, rapidly improving AI cyber capabilities, and steps toward image provenance metadata and watermarks.
